terms: Machine learning
Software that learns patterns from examples instead of following fixed rules.
Model
The learned program that makes predictions or answers.
Training data
The examples used to teach a model.
LLM
A large language model: an AI trained on lots of text to predict and write text.
Agent
An AI system that can take steps, like using tools, to finish a task.
facts: The term 'artificial intelligence' was introduced for a 1956 summer workshop at Dartmouth College.
artificial-intelligence.challenge: Ask an AI tool the same question in two different ways. Which answer was clearer, and why?
change: Writing, coding and design tools may get faster
Routine office tasks may be automated
Knowing how to use AI tools may become a common work skill
opportunity: Do some tasks faster and with less cost
New products and startups built on AI
Roles that combine AI skills with your own field
risk: Some tasks may be automated, changing jobs
AI can give wrong answers with confidence
Rules on data, bias and privacy are still developing

terms: Sensor
A part that lets a robot sense things like light, touch or distance.
Actuator
A part, like a motor, that makes a robot move.
Autonomous
Able to act without a person controlling every move.
Humanoid
A robot shaped roughly like a human.
facts: The word 'robot' comes from a 1920 play by Karel Čapek. It comes from a Czech word for forced labour.
robotics.challenge: Find 3 machines at home that sense something and then react. What do they sense?
change: Robots may move from factories into warehouses, farms and homes
Machines may take over dull or dangerous tasks
opportunity: Demand for people who build, program and maintain robots
Safer work in risky jobs
Help for elderly care and logistics
risk: Some repetitive jobs may shrink
Robots are costly and still limited in messy real places
Safety and responsibility rules are still being set

terms: Orbit
The curved path an object follows around a planet or star.
Satellite
An object that circles another. The Moon is natural; many others are human-made.
Payload
What a rocket carries, such as a satellite.
Telescope
A tool that collects light so we can see faraway objects.
facts: Sputnik 1, launched in 1957, was the first human-made satellite.
space.challenge: Find out how many people are in space right now, using a trusted space agency website.
change: Launching things to orbit may get cheaper
More satellites may mean better internet, maps and weather data
opportunity: New jobs in satellites, data and engineering
Services built on space data, like farming or disaster alerts
Science discoveries that spark new technology
risk: Space projects are expensive and can fail
More satellites means more space junk
Rules and ownership in space are not settled

terms: Battery
Stores energy in chemical form and releases it as electricity.
Grid
The network that carries electricity from where it is made to where it is used.
Renewable
Energy from sources that do not run out, like sun and wind.
Fusion
Joining small atoms to release energy, the process that powers the Sun.
facts: Edmond Becquerel observed the effect behind solar cells in 1839.
energy.challenge: Look at an electricity bill and find how many units (kWh) your home used last month.
change: Cheaper and better batteries may change cars and power grids
More power may come from sun and wind
opportunity: Jobs in clean energy, grid and battery work
Lower energy bills over time if costs fall
New business in storage and charging
risk: Old energy jobs may change
Some new technology may not scale or stay costly
Mining and materials can harm the environment

terms: DNA
The molecule that carries instructions for building living things.
Gene
A section of DNA with instructions for one job, like making a protein.
CRISPR
A tool that can edit DNA at chosen spots.
Protein
A molecule that does most of the work in cells.
facts: The Human Genome Project finished its work in 2003.
biotechnology.challenge: Find one medicine or food that is made using biotechnology.
change: Gene tools may treat some diseases that are hard to treat today
opportunity: Careers in biology, data and medicine
New treatments and better diagnosis
Biotech startups and research roles
risk: Treatments can be very costly at first
Ethics questions about editing genes
Safety testing takes years

terms: Semiconductor
A material that can switch between carrying and blocking electricity. Chips are built from it.
Transistor
A tiny switch inside a chip. Modern chips hold billions.
Nanometre
One billionth of a metre, used to describe tiny chip features.
GPU
A chip that does many simple calculations at once, useful for graphics and AI.
facts: The first transistor was demonstrated at Bell Labs in 1947.
semiconductors.challenge: Count how many devices around you contain a chip.
change: Chips are becoming more important to every industry
Countries and companies are investing in making chips
opportunity: Jobs in chip design and manufacturing
Faster, cheaper devices
New products that need special chips
risk: Supply can be disrupted by shortages or politics
Building chip factories is very costly
Few companies control key steps

terms: Qubit
The quantum version of a bit. It can be in a mix of 0 and 1.
Superposition
Being in a mix of states until measured.
Entanglement
A link between particles: measuring one tells you about the other.
Error correction
Methods to protect fragile quantum information from mistakes.
facts: Quantum computers are not just faster normal computers. They are expected to help only with certain kinds of problems.
quantum-computing.challenge: In your own words, explain why a spinning coin is a rough (not exact) picture of superposition.
change: Quantum computers may help with some chemistry, materials and optimisation problems
Today's lock-and-key security may need to be upgraded
opportunity: Early skills in quantum software and physics
New research and startup fields
Better materials and medicines in the long run
risk: The technology is still early and may take many years
Hype can exceed real results
Future machines may break some current encryption

terms: Encryption
Scrambling data so only someone with the key can read it.
Phishing
Fake messages that trick you into giving away passwords or money.
Two-factor login
A second proof of identity, on top of your password.
Vulnerability
A weakness in software that attackers might use.
facts: The Morris worm, in 1988, was one of the first computer worms to spread widely on the internet.
cybersecurity.challenge: Turn on two-factor login for one important account today.
change: Attacks and defences are both using automation
Organisations are asked to protect data more strictly
opportunity: Strong demand for security skills
Safer systems earn customer trust
Opportunities in training and tools
risk: Data theft and fraud can cost money and trust
One weak password or fake message can cause damage
Defences must keep up with new tricks

terms: 3D printing
Building an object layer by layer from a digital design.
Automation
Machines doing tasks with little human input.
Prototype
A first test version of a product.
Materials science
Studying and designing the stuff things are made of.
facts: Chuck Hull patented stereolithography, an early 3D printing method, in 1986.
advanced-manufacturing.challenge: Pick an everyday object and guess how many steps it takes to make it.
change: Products may be made closer to customers
Small batches and custom items may become cheaper
opportunity: Jobs in automation, design and repair
Faster testing of new product ideas
Small makers can compete with large firms
risk: Some factory jobs may change
Machines and training cost money
Quality and safety checks are still needed
